final.title: Where a knowledge assistant fits, and where it does not
final.body:
A knowledge assistant is not a general answer machine. For a small business, it is only a good fit when the question can be answered from approved company documents you already control. That usually means text-based material such as policies, FAQs, product notes, or other internal references. If the task needs open-web research, fresh judgment, or a human sign-off, you are no longer looking at a knowledge-assistant problem.

That is the practical filter I would use when comparing manual work, hiring, or a bounded automation investment. Bareni’s self-built demo shows the mechanics of one grounded assistant: it can ingest MD, PDF, and URL content, run vector search and reranking, generate answers grounded in company material, and show sources. It is a local demo on synthetic data, with a locked public route; it does not imply production use, customer validation, billing, or proven scale.

The simplest test is this: can your team answer the question by looking in your own documents, or do they need to research outside? If the answer is outside research, the assistant is probably the wrong tool. If the answer is inside your documents, audit one recurring workflow against that threshold and see whether it is a candidate for grounded assistance.

final.title: The real limit of a knowledge assistant
final.body:
A knowledge assistant is useful only when the answer lives in your own approved documents. That is the practical line I’d use in a small business: if the question can be answered from policies, FAQs, product notes, or other text you already control, the assistant may be a fit. If it needs open-web research, judgment, or human sign-off, it is not a knowledge-assistant problem. It is a workflow problem, and software alone will not finish it.

That matters if you are weighing manual work, hiring, or a bounded automation investment. Bareni’s self-built demo is intentionally narrow: it can ingest MD, PDF, and URL content, run vector search and reranking, generate grounded answers, and show sources. It does not prove production use, customer validation, billing, or scale, and it should not be treated as a shortcut around approval.

The test is simple: “Could my team answer this by looking in our own documents, or do they need to research outside?” If the honest answer is outside research, the assistant is probably the wrong tool. If it is inside your documents, audit one recurring workflow against that threshold and see whether it is a candidate for grounded search.
